Navigating Headwinds 
with Agility and Unyielding 
Discipline
FY26 rigorously tested our 
organisational flexibility and our 
stress threshold. We began the year 
facing a confluence of severe external 
disruptions. These included profound 
geopolitical shifts that disrupted 
global logistics networks, extreme 
volatility in raw material prices, 
particularly sharp, unpredictable 
corrections in upstream derivatives 
such as benzene and aniline, and 
the sudden imposition of new U.S. 
tariffs that threatened our established 
export corridors.
Rather than adopting a defensive 
posture or waiting for the macro-
environment to naturally correct 
itself, we relied heavily on our 
execution discipline. We initiated 
comprehensive, structural cost-
optimisation programmes across our 
entire value chain. By establishing 
a lean, highly efficient operational 
baseline, optimising our procurement 
strategies, and implementing dynamic 
pricing models, we successfully 
limited the deterioration in profitability 
during the most volatile quarters. 
This is reflected in EBITDA margins 
stabilising at ~13% to 14% and 
improving sequentially in the second 
half of the year. 
When faced with localised 
disruptions, our commercial teams 
demonstrated remarkable agility. 
They swiftly recalibrated global trade 
flows, actively scaling our presence 
and market share in Europe, the 
Middle East, and Africa to offset 
localised softness elsewhere. We did 
not abandon our key markets; instead, 
we worked collaboratively with our 
North American partners to actively 
absorb parts of the new U.S. tariffs. 
Exports accounted for approximately 
57% of total revenues, with the 
U.S. market experiencing a gradual 
recovery in volumes during the year. 
Internally, we focused relentlessly on 
future-proofing our enterprise against 
inevitable future shocks. By deploying 
advanced Artificial Intelligence 
(AI), digital twins, and predictive 
maintenance tools across our critical 
process blocks, we have transitioned 
from reactive to proactive plant 
management. 
We are now driving measurable 
gains, including:
100+ Cr (Variable and Fixed) cost

30%+ Y-o-Y Volume growth

our baseline operating costs while 
simultaneously achieving our carbon 
footprint reduction targets. 
Accelerating Our 
Green Transition: 
We are on track to have our hybrid 
renewable energy portfolio exceed 
75% of our total power purchases 
across key facilities by Q1 FY27, while 
significantly reducing our carbon 
footprint and operating costs.
Evolving in a Dynamic Global 
Landscape
As the year progressed, we witnessed 
profound structural shifts in global 
trade that strategically favour India 
as a manufacturing hub and AIL, 
specifically, as a preferred partner. 
The successful conclusion of the 
India-EU Free Trade Agreement (FTA) 
and positive, ongoing developments 
in U.S.-India trade dynamics are 
structurally lowering tariff barriers 
for high-end specialty chemicals, 
opening up entirely new, highly 
lucrative corridors for our Advanced 
Materials portfolio. We are actively 
engaging with customers across 
these regions, with a strong pipeline of 
product qualifications and commercial 
discussions underway. 
We are also closely monitoring 
China’s evolving industrial policy. 
Historically, excess capacity and 
aggressive export pricing impacted 
global margins. Recent policy shifts 
aimed at rationalising domestic 
competition are expected to restore 
pricing discipline. We expect gradual 
normalisation in pricing over the next 
12-24 months, supporting margin 
recovery for global specialty chemical 
players. 
In this environment, customer 
expectations are evolving from 
transactional sourcing to strategic 
partnerships. Our integrated value 
chain model positions us strongly 
to deliver reliability, compliance, and 
supply chain resilience.
Delivering Value: Sweating 
Assets and Monumental 
Strategic Wins
Our financial and operational 
momentum recovered strongly as we 
progressed through FY26, a direct 
result of our conscious strategy 
to maximise throughput from our 
existing assets. We improved asset 
turns and increased utilisation across 
key product chains. 
Our energy-linked portfolio, 
particularly MMA, achieved its 
highest-ever volumes. We are scaling 
fuel additives capacities from 290 
KTPA to 360 KTPA by year-end.

dynamics, our ability to 
seamlessly partner with 
global innovators, local 
suppliers, and international 
customers has proven to be 
our strongest strategic moat. 
We are not just supplying 
chemicals; we are co-creating 
absolute supply chain 
resilience.”

What Drives 
At Aarti Industries, 
the ESG strategy 
is guided by 
a materiality 
assessment that 
identifies the 
environmental, 
social, and 
governance issues 
most relevant to 
long-term value 
creation. The 
process is built on 
stakeholder inputs, 
bringing together 
diverse perspectives 
to define priorities 
and focus action

The assessment is reviewed 
annually to remain aligned with 
strategic priorities, emerging risks, 
and regulatory developments. In 
addition, a comprehensive evaluation 
is undertaken every three years, 
incorporating inputs from internal 
and external stakeholders.
Since fiscal year 2019, we have conducted these assessments annually. In 
FY24, we conducted a double materiality assessment based on the GRI 2021 
framework, collaborating with a third-party consultant to gather insights from 
our stakeholders. 
In FY26, the identified material topics were reassessed for both impact and 
financial relevance, with no changes identified. Accordingly, the materiality 
matrix remained unchanged. 
The Company engaged extensively with stakeholders to gather their insights 
on the material issues for its ESG strategy. The materiality assessment is 
subsequently reviewed and approved by the Finance and Investment Committee 
prior to the sign off by the Board of Directors. 
Understanding Double Materiality
Financial Materiality:
Assesses how external 
factors influence the 
Company’s financial 
performance, including 
related risks and 
opportunities (outside-in), 
across the short, medium, 
and long term.
Impact Materiality:
Assesses how the 
Company’s operations affect 
people, society, and the 
environment (inside-out), 
across the short, medium, 
and long term.
Approach to Double Materiality
AIL’s double materiality framework enables the Company to identify and 
prioritise ESG issues and opportunities that are relevant to both business 
performance and stakeholder impact.
The assessment is aligned with the GRI Standards 2021 and the Corporate 
Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD). Since FY24, it reflects a dual 
perspective, covering both impact and financial materiality, and linking ESG 
priorities to long-term value creation.

safety, environmental degradation, and brand reputation. AIL relies on continuous scenario modelling, stress testing, and 
industry benchmarking to validate mitigation barriers against volatility. Our Risk Appetite Framework sets clear tolerance

Commitment to Responsible Chemical Management for utilisation of hazardous substance: We are committed to 
minimising, restricting, and where feasible, eliminating the use of hazardous substances that may pose risks to 
human health and the environment. We comply with all applicable national and international regulations governing the 
manufacture, handling, storage, transportation, use, and disposal of hazardous chemicals, including relevant Indian 
regulatory requirements and globally recognised frameworks where applicable. Our approach emphasises responsible 
chemical management across the entire product life cycle, from raw material sourcing and manufacturing to distribution, 
use, and end-of-life disposal. We continuously assess opportunities to substitute hazardous substances with safer 
alternatives, strengthen operational controls, enhance employee awareness and training, and implement robust risk 
management practices to prevent environmental releases and occupational exposure. Through periodic monitoring, 
regulatory compliance reviews, and continuous improvement initiatives, we strive to reduce the environmental and health 
impacts associated with hazardous substances while ensuring safe and sustainable operations.

Human Rights Due Diligence
A robust human rights due diligence process aligned with UNGP and SA8000 standards is maintained by the Company to 
identify risks across operations, supply chains, partnerships, and mergers.
It addresses key issues including child and forced labour, human trafficking, wages, discrimination, exploitation, freedom of 
association and right to collective bargaining, while also assessing legal penalties. The process incorporates stakeholders 
such as women, children, migrants, contract workers, indigenous peoples, and communities, integrating their concerns to 
build trust.
In FY26, 100% of manufacturing sites across 16 divisions were assessed on human rights. Third-party validation reported 
no major violations or corrective actions. A Zone-level risk register tracks all human rights risks.

reinforced through targeted training. Security teams undergo regular sessions 
on human rights, legal compliance, conflict resolution, soft skills, and crowd 
management. This is further supported by online refresher courses, with 100% 
completion achieved.
To further strengthen accountability, a Disciplinary Action Plan defines 
responses to violations, discrimination, and harassment, while deterring 
misconduct. All investigations are led by the CHRO, who also serves as the 
Ethics Officer.

SUCCESS STORY 
Module-based Training for Shift In-Charges and DCS Executives
Shift In-Charges and DCS Executives play a critical role in ensuring safe, stable and efficient plant operations. 
Internal reviews showed that while they managed daily operations effectively, their exposure to key aspects 
of the Aarti Management System was limited. Production demands, troubleshooting and coordination 
responsibilities left little time to revisit structured management system expectations, risk frameworks and 
standardised practices. This created the possibility of variation in system-led decision-making across shifts.
Structured Intervention
To address this gap, AIL introduced a module-based 
training programme for Shift In-Charges and DCS 
Executives. Participants were relieved of their regular 
duties for 8 hours once every 4 months, enabling 
focused learning without operational distractions.
The programme covered four modules and more 
than 80 technical and system-related topics aligned 
with critical AMS elements. Over 400 employees 
were covered, with sessions repeated every 
four months to reinforce recall, consistency and 
application across shifts.
Areas of Learning
The sessions strengthened understanding of 
critical process parameters, interlock logic, alarm 
management, deviation control and structured risk 
assessment in line with AMS expectations. Real 
plant scenarios and past incident case studies made 
the learning practical and relevant. Participants 
were encouraged to move beyond immediate 
troubleshooting and adopt a system-driven 
approach to process control, operating discipline 
and risk anticipation.
The initiative improved confidence, ownership and alignment with AMS requirements among 
Shift In-Charges and DCS Executives. By linking daily operating decisions with management system 
principles, it strengthened process discipline, enhanced operational reliability and reinforced a proactive 
safety culture across the organisation.

The assessment and appointment of Board members prioritise ethics, personal and professional stature, domain expertise,

weight) and ROIC (40% weight). The NRC Committee has the authority to adjust performance targets to reflect market 
conditions and economic factors.
The CEO’s compensation comprises fixed pay, variable pay, and long-term incentives linked to strategic and financial 
metrics like profitability, EBITDA, and ROCE, aligning leadership with sustainable shareholder value.

candidate separately.

 ECONOMIC OVERVIEW
Global Economy
The 
macroeconomic environment reflected moderate 
growth amid evolving policy, trade and geopolitical 
dynamics. According to the IMF’s World Economic Outlook, 
April 2026, global growth stabilised at 3.1%. However, this 
headline stability masked a deeper structural shift, as 
economies continued to adjust to the delayed effects of 
monetary tightening, shifting inflation trends, and a more 
policy-led global trade environment.
These conditions also influenced the global speciality 
chemicals industry. Following the prolonged inventory 
destocking cycle witnessed during 2023-25, the industry 
entered CY 2025 on a more normalised footing. As inventory 
levels stabilised across end-user industries, demand 
visibility improved selectively. This was particularly evident 
in areas linked to replacement cycles in agrochemicals 
and secular growth in high-performance polymers and 
electronics.
At the same time, global trade flows increasingly reflected 
what McKinsey describes as ‘The Great Re-shoring’. 
Industrial policy, supply security and geopolitical alignment 
became as important as cost competitiveness. Persistent 
regional tensions and evolving trade alliances gradually 
shifted corporate priorities from ‘Just-in-Time’ efficiency 
to ‘Just-in-Case’ resilience. This transition strengthened 
the relevance of dependable manufacturing partners. 
Companies such as AIL remained well-positioned as safe-
harbour partners for global MNCs seeking to de-risk supply 
chains, diversify sourcing and improve long-term continuity.
Supply-side conditions remained broadly stable, although 
intermittent geopolitical developments continued to create 
volatility in energy prices, logistics, and trade flows. In 
response, companies placed greater emphasis on supply 
chain diversification, regional partnerships and resource 
optimisation. This strengthened collaboration across

global trade uncertainties and financial market volatility.

the year, supported by prudent fiscal management and a 
well-calibrated monetary policy environment.

INDUSTRY OVERVIEW
Global Chemical Industry
The 
global chemical industry entered 2026 amid subdued 
economic growth, elevated geopolitical tensions and the 
lingering effects of prolonged inventory destocking across 
several end-user sectors. Growth expectations for the global 
chemicals industry moderated from earlier projections 
as weaker industrial activity, trade uncertainty, tariffs and 
sanctions affected demand visibility and influenced long-
term sourcing strategies.
However, the industry also began moving beyond the post-
2022 cyclical correction that started in early 2023. As 
inventory levels normalised across key value chains, the 
recovery became increasingly selective rather than broad-
based. This led to the emergence of a two-speed growth 
model within the sector.

184 Integrated Annual Report 2025-26
Commodity and bulk chemicals continued to face pressure 
from overcapacity, intense competition and margin 
compression. These challenges were driven largely by 
China’s significant capacity additions over the past few 
years. The additional capacities altered global trade flows 
and created medium- to long-term competitive pressure 
across several end applications.
In contrast, speciality and knowledge-led chemicals 
demonstrated stronger resilience. Growth in these 
segments was supported by higher-value applications 
and customer-specific solutions. These segments are 
estimated to grow at nearly 1.5 times the rate of GDP growth, 
driven by structural demand from the energy transition, 
electric vehicles, semiconductor localisation, sustainable 
agriculture, electronics, high-performance polymers, and 
advanced manufacturing.
The growing need for performance-driven materials and 
application-specific solutions continued to support value-
added product categories. At the same time, traditional 
bulk chemical segments experienced relatively subdued 
demand.
These trends extended the industry’s recovery timeline 
while increasing differentiation across product categories 
and business models. Companies focused on specialised 
chemistries, customer intimacy, technical capabilities and 
innovation-led portfolios demonstrated relatively stronger 
growth and profitability. As a result, collaboration became 
increasingly central to value creation. Companies continued 
to co-develop products with customers, form strategic 
alliances and integrate across value chains to enhance 
competitiveness.
In an uncertain and volatile environment, global companies 
also adopted multifold strategies to strengthen supply 
chain resilience and reduce dependence on concentrated 
sourcing ecosystems. This accelerated a shift from ‘Just-in-
Time’ efficiency to ‘Just-in-Case’ preparedness. Companies 
increasingly prioritised supplier diversification, inventory 
flexibility, regional sourcing options and long-term supply 
assurance.
This realignment received further support from China’s anti-
involution drive, which aims to curb irrational price wars 
and excessive capacity-led competition. For India, as an 
emerging alternative sourcing partner for various chemical 
products, this presents a significant opportunity to establish 
itself as a preferred global hub for chemicals and speciality 
manufacturing.
Sustainability also became a fundamental strategic priority 
for the industry. The transition towards greener and more 
circular solutions is creating a sizeable market opportunity 
for new-age chemicals, including bio-based products, 
advanced circular materials and sustainable process 
technologies.
Companies continued to accelerate investments in green 
chemistry, recycling technologies and sustainable product 
lines in response to tightening regulations and evolving 
customer preferences. At the same time, supply chain 
optimisation and strategic collaborations gained further 
importance, as industry participants worked to improve 
resilience while aligning with emerging circular economy 
principles.

Outlook
Despite cyclical challenges, structural demand drivers 
continue 
to support the chemical industry’s long-
term outlook. Demand growth remains driven by 
urbanisation, infrastructure development, electric 
mobility, semiconductors, renewable energy, healthcare, 
electronics, agriculture, and consumer goods. Speciality 
chemicals continue to demonstrate greater resilience than 
commodity chemicals. This is primarily due to higher value 
addition, customised applications, and stronger customer 
integration.
Reflecting these underlying drivers, the sector’s long-term 
outlook remains positive. According to projections from 
ACC and ICCA, the global chemical industry is expected to 
grow by 3-4%, broadly in line with overall economic activity. 
However, the growth trajectory is likely to remain uneven 
across regions and segments.
In the near term, commodity chemicals may continue to 
face pressure due to soft demand and excess capacity. 
Over the medium term, speciality chemicals are expected 
to witness stronger growth. This trend is already visible in 
sectors such as electronics, clean energy, and advanced 
manufacturing, as highlighted by McKinsey and Deloitte 
(FY 2024-25).
At the same time, shifts in global supply chains are expected 
to gradually rebalance production towards emerging hubs 
such as India. Existing manufacturing hubs, including 
those in Europe, continue to face structural disadvantages 
stemming from high energy costs. This has led to ongoing 
asset rationalisation across the region. 
Sustainability considerations, including investments in 
green chemistry and low-carbon processes, are also 
expected to play a more central role in shaping long-
term competitiveness. Overall, industry performance will 
depend on product mix, geographic positioning, and the 
ability to adapt to evolving geopolitical and environmental 
requirements.
Indian Chemical Industry
The Indian chemical industry continued to demonstrate 
resilience during FY 2025-26 despite a challenging global 
environment. The sector faced demand moderation, 
overcapacity in commodity chemicals, volatile feedstock 
prices, and geopolitical uncertainties. However, strong 
domestic demand, rising export opportunities, and 
increasing supply-chain diversification continued to support 
growth. As a result, India strengthened its position as a 
strategically important manufacturing destination.
Driven by these favourable dynamics, the sector’s economic 
footprint is expanding rapidly. The industry is currently 
estimated at USD 155-165 billion and is projected to reach 
USD 230-255 billion by 2030, implying a CAGR of around 
8-9%. The sector remains highly diversified and includes 
petrochemicals, speciality chemicals, agrochemicals, 
and pharmaceuticals, amongst others. It also continues 
to contribute meaningfully to India’s industrial output and 
manufacturing value addition.
India’s speciality chemicals segment remains a key 
growth engine for the industry. Demand from automobiles, 
electronics, construction chemicals, pharmaceuticals, 
personal care, water treatment, and renewable energy 
sectors is expected to support continued investments in 
value-added downstream products.
This multi-sectoral demand for speciality chemicals has 
created a resilient manufacturing ecosystem. In turn, this 
ecosystem serves as a strong foundation for international 
expansion. Leveraging this domestic strength, India has 
positioned itself as a key alternative manufacturing hub. 
The country also stands to benefit significantly from 
the forthcoming implementation of India-UK, India-EU, 
and India-Oman FTA arrangements. Furthermore, cost 
competitiveness, a skilled workforce, and improved 
infrastructure continue to drive this shift.

This structural shift is accelerating the need for a 
collaborative ecosystem. In this environment, integrated 
players like Aarti Industries can partner with global 
customers and stakeholders to deliver reliable, scalable, 
and innovation-led solutions.
Outlook
The industry’s growth remains resilient, supported by 
rising 
domestic consumption, infrastructure development,

The implementation of various cross-border FTAs and trade 
agreements positions India as a suitable and preferred

India 
is strategically positioned to benefit from several 
structural and cyclical opportunities emerging across the 
global chemical value chain.
1. Supply Chain Diversification and Supply-Side 
Rationalisation: China’s policy shift to curb excess 
capacity is expected to create a more rational global 
pricing environment. This trend is likely to benefit 
integrated and collaborative players, which offer long-
term partnerships and supply chain reliability. 
2. Trade Agreements: The India-EU FTA and the US-India 
trade deal are expected to boost export volumes and 
provide long-term earnings visibility. 
3. Sunrise Sectors: Increasing applications in Electric 
Vehicles (EVs), renewable energy, and chemical 
recycling present significant growth avenues. 
4. Import Substitution: India continues to import several 
petrochemical intermediates and speciality chemicals, 
creating opportunities for domestic capacity 
expansion.
5. Green Chemistry: The global shift toward sustainable 
and bio-based chemicals creates opportunities for 
Indian players to expand into environmentally friendly 
products.

manufacturing improves efficiency through process 
optimisation.
7. PLI Schemes and Policy Support: PLI schemes and 
other manufacturing-focused policy measures are 
strengthening India’s competitiveness across priority 
sectors. For the chemical industry, these initiatives 
encourage domestic manufacturing, improve 
scale, attract investments and support higher-value 
production. This is especially relevant for sectors 
linked to electronics, clean energy, advanced materials 
and import substitution.

COMPANY OVERVIEW
Aarti Industries Limited (‘AIL’ or ‘the Company’) is a leading 
global 
speciality chemicals company. It is renowned for 
its expertise in benzene and toluene-based derivatives. 
The Company is also a leading manufacturer and exporter 
of speciality chemicals used primarily as performance-
enhancing octane boosters in the energy sector.
Headquartered in Mumbai, India, the Company was 
established in 1984 by first-generation technocrats. Over 
the past four decades, AIL has evolved into a recognised 
‘Global Partner of Choice’. This position is driven by its 
ability to collaborate with global customers across the 
product lifecycle, from concept to commercialisation.
AIL’s evolution is anchored in the ‘Chemistry of 
Collaboration’. Through integrated, strategic partnerships 
with customers, suppliers, and other partners, the Company 
co-creates solutions, optimises processes, and delivers 
long-term value. This approach enables customised delivery 
capabilities while maintaining cost efficiency.
The Company’s competitive advantage is built on a strong 
foundation of integrated operations, process chemistry 
scale-up expertise, and a strategically distributed network 
of research and development (R&D) and pilot plants. AIL 
ranks 4th globally for approximately 75% of its product 
portfolio, serving over 1,100 customers across more than 
60 countries.
Today, AIL has a significant presence across India, the 
Middle East, North America, Europe, and other international 
markets. The Company offers customised and novel 
delivery solutions, including near-to-plant stock points, to 
support key market requirements.
AIL is recognised as a leader in chlorination, nitration, and 
hydrogenation chemistries. It leverages key raw materials 
to drive innovation and strengthen its position in speciality 
chemicals. The Company’s core operations are centred on 
key value chains, including Nitro Chloro Benzenes (NCB), 
Dichlorobenzenes (DCB), Phenylenediamines (PDA), and 
Nitro Toluene (NT).
These intermediates support downstream applications 
across agrochemicals, pharmaceuticals, polymers, aFuel 
additives, dyes and pigments. During the year, AIL continued 
its strategic shift from bulk product manufacturing to a 
knowledge-driven, application-led solutions provider. This 
transition reflects the expansion of high-value chemistries 
and deeper customer engagement through chemistry-led 
and R&D-oriented solutions.
Increasingly, AIL is evolving from a product-led organisation 
to a platform-led speciality chemicals company. 
Through integrated chemistry platforms, multipurpose 
manufacturing assets, process development expertise and 
customer co-creation capabilities, the Company is building 
scalable growth engines capable of serving multiple end-
use sectors and application areas. This platform-led 
approach enables faster commercialisation, improved 
asset utilisation and deeper strategic engagement with 
global customers.
AIL further strengthened its position through deeper 
backward integration and improved global supply chain

cycle, the agrochemicals segment showed signs of a stable 
recovery in FY 2025-26. While volumes remained stable for 
most of the year, notable growth was witnessed in NT and 
the downstream ethylation chain of products, while pricing 
remained subdued due to competitive pressures from 
China. 
• Strategic Partnerships: AIL secured a USD 150 
million medium-term supply contract with a global 
agrochemical major in March 2026, for a critical 
intermediate used in crop protection formulations, 
marking a significant milestone in long-term 
collaborative growth. The contract extends to March 
2030 and would be met with existing capacities 
• Forward Integration: The PEDA project, a forward 
integration ethylation project at Zone IV is under 
commissioning trials, with a capacity of 4,000 TPA, 
strengthening India’s agrochemical self-reliance and 
providing AIL with a significant cost advantage 
Dyes, Pigments, and Printing Inks
Demand in this segment remained steady throughout the 
year, with volumes expected to improve as global demand 
for textiles and printing revives. However, one of the core 
products, 3,3-DCBH, continued to face global demand 
pressure due to a sharp increase in product prices, driven 
by higher raw material costs and elevated freight rates. The 
impact is expected to be partly offset by improving demand 
in the Indian market. Applications across dyes, pigments, 
and printing inks continued to generate steady cash flows, 
supported by a refined pricing strategy that balanced 
volume growth with margin preservation. 
Polymers and Additives
PDCB demand grew due to its application in the EV sector, 
even as the polymers segment experienced mixed trends. 
However, other polymer additive chains faced pressure in 
the US market. This prompted the Company to respond

BUSINESS HIGHLIGHTS
FY 2025-26 marked a year of steady strategic progress for 
AIL 
despite a volatile global environment characterised 
by geopolitical tensions, supply chain disruptions, raw 
material volatility and sustained competitive pressures. The 
Company continued to strengthen its long-term positioning 
through capacity expansion, medium to long-term contracts, 
backward integration initiatives and portfolio diversification 
into higher-value speciality chemicals.
A key strategic milestone was a ₹ 200-250 Crs backwards-
integration capex initiative with a global customer, aimed 
at strengthening integration for the key product under the 
residual 15-year long-term contract structure. 
Another one is the USD 150 million supply agreement with 
a global agrochemical innovator, extending through March 
2030, which enhances long-term revenue visibility without 
incremental capex. 
The Company secured long-term methanol and toluene 
feedstock contracts across GCC and Southeast Asia, 
improving raw material security and cost predictability, and 
entered a strategic chlorine supply partnership with DCM 
Shriram Limited to support its Zone IV Jhagadia facility 
through dedicated pipeline infrastructure.
The Company also advanced its portfolio expansion 
through partnerships, including the exclusive PCBTF 
distribution agreement with Actylis. It further progressed 
joint ventures, including Augene (Superform JV) and the 
recycling-focused Re Aarti platform, all of which remain on 
track for commissioning in FY 27.
From a segment perspective, agrochemicals and pharma 
remained stable in volume but continued to face margin 
pressure due to global oversupply and Chinese competition. 
Among Polymers, EV-linked demand remained a strong 
contributor to growth, while dyes and pigments were 
relatively stable, supported by resilient domestic demand.
Capex during FY 2025-26 stood at about ₹ 1,125 Crs, 
primarily directed towards Zone IV expansion and fast-track 
capacity additions such as MMA, DCB and PEDA-related 
initiatives. This reflects the tail end of a high-investment 
cycle, with management indicating a transition towards 
lower capex intensity in FY 2026-27 as major projects near 
completion.
Zone IV remained the flagship growth platform, with the 
Calcium Chloride unit commercialised and ramping up, 
while other blocks, including the multipurpose plant and 
PEDA, progressed through commissioning stages, albeit 
with short-term delays, supporting the shift towards higher-
value product streams.
FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE
FY 2025-26 was marked by a challenging operating 
environment characterised by raw material volatility, 
geopolitical disruptions, elevated freight costs, logistics 
bottlenecks and continued competitive pressure from 
Chinese suppliers. Uncertainty relating to US tariffs on 
Indian chemical exports and broader supply chain disruptions 
also weighed on industry conditions during the year. 
Despite this backdrop, the Company delivered a 
resilient performance with revenue rising 12% YoY to 
₹ 9,018 Crs, supported by volume growth, improving 
capacity utilisation, recovery in export volumes, and stable 
domestic demand. Additionally, higher-margin, value-added 
products contributed to overall growth.
EBITDA increased over 15% YoY to ₹ 1,172 Crs, driven by 
operating leverage, cost optimisation initiatives, and scale 
benefits from higher utilisation. Profitability was partly 
impacted by inventory valuation losses, shipment-related 
disruptions, and one-time labour code implementation 
costs of ₹ 15 Crs, though efficiency gains supported gradual 
improvement through the year. The increasing share 
of long-term customer engagements and collaborative 
business models is expected to enhance revenue visibility 
and support margin stability over the medium term.
Finance costs noted accounting adjustments. FY 2025-26 
saw mixed forex impacts, including gains of ~₹ 16 Crs (Q1) 
and ~₹ 10 Crs (Q4), offset by a ₹ 34 Crs mark-to-market 
loss on ECBs (Q2) and a ₹ 39 Crs revaluation loss on an 
unhedged foreign currency loan (Q4). These are non-
cash accounting impacts, highlighting the natural hedge 
provided by the Company’s export profile over the long-term 
repayment cycle. Depreciation remained as expected, with 
potential tax-efficiency benefits as new capacities come 
online.
PAT for FY 2025-26 increased 27% YoY to ₹ 419 Crs, 
supported by stronger operating performance and 
improved leverage, despite forex-related impacts and other 
exceptional items.

Capital Expenditure
FY 2025-26 capex stood at ₹ 1,125 Crs, marking the peak 
phase of investment in the Zone IV platform development. 
During the year, key assets such as the calcium chloride 
plant, multipurpose plant (MPP), 4,000 TPA PEDA facility, 
and related downstream units advanced through various 
commissioning stages. However, execution timelines 
were delayed by 3-4 months due to labour constraints, 
commercial LPG availability issues, and election-related 
workforce migration. As a result, while the calcium chloride 
plant has completed commercial runs and is currently 
ramping up, the MPP and PEDA facilities continue to 
undergo commissioning trials.
For FY 2026-27, capex is expected to moderate to ₹ 750-
800 Crs as the Company shifts from a heavy investment 
phase towards optimisation and execution-led growth. 
The Zone IV platform, forming part of a total build-out of 
₹ 1,600-1,800 Crs, is now entering its revenue-generation 
phase. Initial commercial revenue aggregation from these 
assets is expected to commence in the second half of 
FY 2026-27. Thereafter, revenue contribution is likely to 
increase gradually as operations stabilise and utilisation 
levels improve.
BUSINESS OUTLOOK
The near-term outlook is expected to benefit from improved 
capacity 
utilisation, healthy visibility of long-term contracts 
and continued execution of integration-led initiatives. The 
Company expects gradual deleveraging, with net debt likely 
to moderate this year through operating improvements and 
sustained efficiency measures. Margin expansion is also 
expected to be supported by operating leverage and cost 
optimisation initiatives.
For FY 2026-27, the capex cycle is expected to enter a 
low-intensity phase, with spending projected to decline 
significantly to well below ₹ 1,000 Crs due to the absence 
of major greenfield projects. The effective tax rate is 
also expected to normalise within the 9-15% range. 
Operationally, key milestones include commissioning the 
Zone IV facilities during FY 2026-27, with initial revenue 
contributions expected in the second half of the year, as 
well as commissioning the JVs. Additional support may 
also arise from external demand-supply dynamics, including 
potential benefits from shifts in the Chinese chemical 
market, beginning FY 2026-27.
Aarti Industries is steadily shifting its portfolio towards 
higher-margin, innovation-led segments, with greater focus 
on advanced materials and speciality chemistries, while 
reducing dependence on commoditised bulk chemicals. 
This transition is being strengthened through deeper CDMO 
engagement, including multiple early-stage collaborations 
with global innovators. R&D efforts remain focused on 
advanced materials, polymer science and emerging 
application areas, supported by AI-led tools and digital 
manufacturing initiatives to improve process efficiency, 
energy intensity and operational reliability.
Alongside this strategic evolution, the Company has 
strengthened its ESG and people credentials. It received an 
EcoVadis platinum rating (Top 1%) and was included in the 
CDP – A List for climate performance. The Company also 
recently won the Gallup Exceptional Workplace Award 2026, 
becoming one of the first Indian manufacturing companies 
to receive this recognition. Collectively, these achievements 
reflect the Company’s growing focus on sustainability, 
governance quality and organisational capability, alongside 
its ongoing business transformation.

31. ENVIRONMENT
 The Company is committed to advancing 
envir
onmental stewardship by embedding robust 
environmental management practices, strengthening 
climate resilience, and promoting responsible 
resource utilisation across its operations. Through a 
structured Environmental and Waste Management 
framework, we continuously enhance operational 
efficiency while minimising our environmental 
footprint and dependence on natural resources. Water 
stewardship and advanced effluent management 
remain key material priorities, supported by 
continuous investments in process optimisation 
and resource recovery initiatives. These efforts have 
delivered measurable environmental outcomes, 
including improved effluent quality, enhanced resource 
efficiency, and the transformation of waste streams 
into value-added products, reinforcing our commitment 
to circularity and sustainable operations.
 Water Stewardship
 Recognising water as a critical natural resource, 
Company continues to strengthen its water stewardship 
practices by embedding circular water management 
across its operations. Our comprehensive 3R (Reduce, 
Reuse and Recycle) strategy, supported by a long-term 
vision of achieving Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) across 
all manufacturing facilities, enables us to optimise 
freshwater consumption while enhancing operational 
resilience. During FY 2025–26, we expanded our water 
conservation initiatives through enhanced rainwater 
Board’s Report FSCO
207Aarti Industries Limited
harvesting, increased recovery of MEE and steam 
condensate, 
and higher utilisation of treated sewage 
water and RO permeate. As a result of these sustained 
efforts, eight manufacturing facilities have achieved 
ZLD status and three facilities are ZLD-ready, with 
the remaining sites advancing towards ZLD through 
phased implementation and continuous infrastructure 
enhancements.
 Air Quality and Emission Management
 Company is committed to maintaining high standards 
of air quality management through a proactive 
and technology-driven approach to emission 
control. Advanced pollution abatement systems, 
including wet and dry scrubbers, bag filters, and 
Electrostatic Precipitators (ESPs), are deployed across 
manufacturing facilities to effectively manage process 
and flue gas emissions. Continuous investments 
in process innovation, including dry scrubber 
systems with lime dosing technology, have further 
enhanced sulphur dioxide (SO 2) emission reduction. 
Complementing these efforts, comprehensive Leak 
Detection and Repair (LDAR) programmes minimise 
fugitive emissions and volatile organic compounds 
(VOCs), strengthening operational integrity and 
environmental performance.
 Real-time environmental monitoring is enabled through 
Continuous Emission Monitoring Systems (CEMS) and 
online hazardous gas detection systems installed 
across manufacturing sites, with direct integration 
to CPCB and SPCB regulatory portals to ensure 
regulatory compliance and operational transparency. 
Through these sustained efforts, ambient air quality 
is consistently maintained in accordance with the 
National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS). 
The Company has also completely phased out Ozone 
Depleting Substances (ODS) and confirms that no 
Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs), as defined under 
the Stockholm Convention, are generated through its 
operations, reinforcing its commitment to responsible 
environmental stewardship and sustainable 
manufacturing.
 Waste Management and Circularity
 Waste management at Company is anchored in the 
principles of circularity and responsible resource 
stewardship. Our integrated waste management 
strategy is built on three strategic priorities—source 
reduction, resource recovery through the 4R principle 
(Reuse, Recover, Recycle and Reprocess), and 
environmentally sound disposal. By prioritising co-
processing and other resource recovery pathways over 
conventional landfilling and incineration, we maximise 
waste valorisation while advancing our circular 
economy objectives.
 In FY 2025–26, we diverted 95% of waste away 
from landfill and 13/16 divisions are certified as 
Zero Waste to Landfill. We also enhanced our waste 
governance through the digitalisation of hazardous 
waste monitoring and round-the-clock tracking of 
waste transportation vehicles via the Aarti Logistics 
Control Centre. These initiatives strengthen end-to-
end traceability, improve regulatory compliance, and 
reinforce our commitment to transparent, safe, and 
responsible waste management practices.

A) CONSERVATION FOR ENERGY AND REDUCTION IN 
CARBON EMISSION
 The Steps Taken or Impact on Conservation of Energy;
 To achieve our emission reduction targets validated 
by Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi), our 
multi-disciplinary teams operate through a strategic 
framework anchored by three fundamental pillars: 
Fit for Purpose, Focus to Finish, and Right First Time. 
Our decarbonization roadmap focuses on high-impact 
initiatives such as mitigating energy losses, optimizing 
equipment performance, and refining process 
efficiencies. We are actively transitioning toward 
renewable power sources and alternative fuels while 
integrating cutting-edge technologies to eliminate 
process-related emissions.
 These efforts are supported by a granular approach 
to energy conservation, including the synchronization 
of energy demand and supply, the implementation of 
energy-efficient maintenance protocols, and the use 
of modern monitoring devices to reduce equipment 
idle time. Central to our energy governance is a digital 
Energy Management System (EnMS). This IT-driven 
platform tracks critical electrical metrics and produces 
automated, bespoke reporting, delivering the real-
time insights necessary for agile and effective energy 
management.
 Key energy-saving measures implemented during 
FY 2025-26 across utilities and process systems 
to improve efficiency and reliability are installation 
of VFDs on high-load equipment, performance 
improvement and replacement of water chillers, and 
extensive pump upgrades across cooling water and 
chilled water systems. 
 Additional steps such as impeller modifications to 
avoid throttling, installation of pressure transmitters, 
and new pump installations have optimized system 
performance. Integration and interlocking of chillers, 
pumps, and air compressors further ensured operation 
based on demand, reducing energy wastage. We have 
reduced power consumption by approximately 2.4 
million kWh during FY 2025–26.
 Through process optimization we have recovered 
28,96,712 GJ of steam from the distillation condenser 
during 2025-26, this is an increase of 77% from the 
previous FY. We have regularized usage of Biomass 
for replacing coal gradually in order to reduce carbon 
emissions. 
 Furthermore we have started usage Bio-ethanol 
on a regular mode to move towards elimination of 
conventional liquid fuels
 AIL has commissioned a group captive hybrid 
renewable energy plant for sourcing 13.2 MW of 
renewable power in FY 2023–24, with an investment of 
₹15.18 crore. During the current financial year, AIL has 
reduced approximately 37,000 tCO 2e using renewable 
electricity from this 13.2 MW hybrid plant.
 Further, the Board of AIL has approved Phase-II 
expansion of 25.7 MW hybrid renewable capacity in 
FY 2024-25, out of this 7.9 MW is already commissioned 
and we are receiving electricity from it. We expect 
that the remaining 17.8 MW will be commissioned in 
FY27. Further as part of Phase-III 2.75 MW of wind 
power is being received from November 2025 and we 
have reduced more than 400 tCO 2e using renewable 
electricity from this project. Once all the phases are 
commissioned we will be meeting more than 68% of 
our electricity requirements from renewable sources. 
 We estimate to reduce more than 100,000 mt tCO 2e 
through these initiatives in coming FY.
 The following are the major steps taken during FY 
2025-26 to conserve energy:
 • Zone 1: 
  Installation of VFD’s and linking their speed 
variations to relevant process parameters
  Optimizing usage of air compressor in acid 
and organic divisions
  Replacement and refurbishment of pumps 
  Avoiding flow throttling by reducing flow 
speed through VFD, by replacing impeller etc
  Power saving in ETP by replacing surface 
aeration with diffused aeration for existing 
blowers 
  Revamping the RO to reducing MEE load
  Increasing power generation from CPP by 
creating additional infrastructure
  Energy saving through performance 
improvement and optimization of water 
chilling plant in Topaz division
 • Zone 2:
  Installation of new VAM chiller and 
transitioning from a fixed point to a dew 
point based timer controller.

BOARD OF DIRECTORS - TWO LAYER FRAMEWORK
Aligning with the prevailing regulatory mandate and 
upholding 
the highest standards of the corporate 
governance, structuring the Board of Directors and its 
Committees can be viewed as a functional “Two-Layer” 
framework. This setup allows a Company to divide its 
governance responsibilities between macro-level strategic 
oversight and micro-level technical specialisation.
• Delegation vs. Abdication: While the top layer (the 
Board) delegates specialised tasks to the second 
layer (Committees) to save time and leverage specific 
expertise, the Board cannot abdicate its ultimate 
responsibility. The full Board holds plenary authority 
over corporate governance, strategic direction, 
Company policies and continues to review, approve, 
and formally ratify committee recommendations 
where appropriate. 
• The Power of Independence: Certain critical 
committees; specifically Audit Committee, Nomination 
and remuneration Committee, Risk Management 
Committee, Stakeholders Relationship Committee 
and the CSR Committee - are typically governed by 
the Terms of Reference set for them by the regulators 
including their composition. This ensures that sensitive 
decisions are free from executive bias. The Committees 
conduct the initial deep-dives and present proposals or 
recommendations for the Board to consider. Whereas, 
the Board can make final, legally binding decisions for

• Efficiency and Agility: By utilising this two-layer 
approach, the Board of Directors is the ultimate 
governing body elected by shareholders to oversee 
the Company’s entire Strategy, Management and 
Operations. The committees on the other hand are 
smaller, focused subgroups established by the main 
Board to manage specific, complex governance areas 
and do the heavy lifting beforehand, allowing the full 
Board to focus its limited time on high-level strategy 
and growth.

Board Operations, Digital Transformation, and Committee

To accelerate digital transformation and build a future-
ready enterprise, the Company has systematically 
embedded artificial intelligence (AI) into its leadership 
mandate and operational workflows. Executive Directors

their schedules and ensure meaningful participation. For

Ethics and Fair Business Practices
Company is committed to conducting its business 
operations with absolute honesty, integrity, and fairness. 
This Company has an Ethics and Fair Business Practices 
policy that applies to all Directors, permanent and 
contractual employees, consultants, vendors, and business 
associates acting on behalf of the Company. AIL enforces a 
strict zero-tolerance framework against bribery, kickbacks, 
and facilitation payments of “anything of value.” Political 
contributions are prohibited without explicit Board approval, 
and charitable donations must be for legitimate causes. 
Gifts and hospitality are permitted only if minor, transparent, 
and capped at ` 5,000 per financial year unless expressly 
authorised by the Ethics Committee. Furthermore, the 
policy mandates strict anti-money laundering due diligence, 
zero tolerance for fraudulent activities - subject to severe 
statutory penalties under Section 447 of the Companies 
Act, 2013 - and the mandatory disclosure of any personal 
or familiar conflicts of interest. To preserve fair market 
competition, employees are strictly prohibited from 
engaging in price-fixing, market sharing, or bid-rigging. 
Additionally, the policy rigorously forbids insider trading or 
the unauthorised sharing of Unpublished Price Sensitive 
Information (UPSI).
AIL actively encourages stakeholders to report any 
suspected non-compliance or malpractices immediately to 
ethics.committee@aarti-industries.com or via post to the 
CHRO/Compliance 
Officer at the Mumbai corporate office. 
Backed by a robust Whistleblower framework, the Company 
guarantees strict confidentiality and absolute protection 
against retaliation for any concerns raised in good faith. This 
policy forms an integral part of employment contracts and 
is continuously reinforced across the organisation through 
regular training, discussions, and internal communications.

Saksham Niveshak Campaign
The Company actively participated in the Investor Education 
and Protection Fund Authority’s (IEPFA) “Saksham 
Niveshak” campaign, an investor awareness initiative aimed 
at reducing the volume of unclaimed dividends and shares 
transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund 
(IEPF) in accordance with Section 124(5) of the Companies 
Act, 2013. The campaign sought to encourage shareholders 
to update their KYC and contact details, verify their records, 
and claim their unclaimed dividends and shares before they 
become liable for transfer to the IEPF.
To maximise outreach and shareholder participation, the 
Company undertook a series of awareness initiatives, 
including direct communication through e-mails and letters 
to concerned shareholders, publication of newspaper 
advertisements in English and Gujarati at regular intervals, 
press releases, and dedicated disclosures and awareness 
sections on the Company’s website. These initiatives were 
designed to educate shareholders about the IEPF process, 
applicable timelines, documentation requirements, and the 
procedure for claiming their dues.
The campaign received a positive response from 
shareholders and contributed significantly towards 
enhancing investor awareness and engagement. During the 
campaign period, the Company witnessed an increase in 
requests for claiming unclaimed dividends and shares from 
the IEPF, with approximately 2,000 shareholder requests 
received for share-related claims and dividend claims 
exceeding ` 40 Lakhs. The initiative also facilitated KYC 
updations and improved the accuracy and completeness 
of shareholder records, thereby strengthening investor 
services and shareholder communication.

 viii) Share Transfer process and Dematerialisation:
 In accordance with Regulation 40 of the 
Listing Regulations, as amended from time to 
time, transfer/transmission and transposition 
of securities shall be effected only in 
dematerialised form. Listed companies shall 
issue the securities in dematerialised form. 
Listed companies shall issue the securities in 
dematerialised form only, for processing any 
service request from shareholders viz., issue 
of duplicate share certificates, endorsement, 
transmission, transposition etc. Accordingly, 
Members are requested to make service requests 
by submitting a duly filled and signed Form 
ISR-4/ISR-5, the format of which is available 
on the Company’s website at https://www.
aarti-industries.com/investors/shareholder-
information?category=Shareholder%20Services 
After processing the service request, a letter of 
confirmation will be issued to shareholders and 
shall be valid for a period of 120 days, within 
which the shareholder shall make a request to the 
Depository Participant (‘DP’) for dematerialising 
those shares. If the shareholder fails to submit 
the dematerialisation request within 120 days, 
then the Company shall credit those shares in the 
Suspense Escrow Demat Account (‘SEDA’) held 
by the Company. Shareholders can claim those 
shares transferred to SEDA on submission of 
necessary documentation.

2 Energy 
Management
Opportunity We are committed to a 
decarbonisation strategy 
centred on increasing the share 
of renewable energy within our 
power mix and institutionalising 
energy-efficient solutions 
across our manufacturing 
footprint. By systematically 
reducing our dependence 
on fossil-fuel-based energy, 
we aim to significantly lower 
our Greenhouse Gas (GHG) 
emissions while enhancing 
resource productivity. This 
transition not only supports 
a cleaner environment but 
also drives long-term cost 
optimisation and reinforces our 
operational resilience.
We have regularised usage 
of Biomass for replacing coal 
gradually in order to reduce carbon 
emissions.
We have several energy efficiency 
programmes through process 
optimisation. Under this, one such 
programme is to recover energy 
from a distillation condenser in 
the form of steam by supplying 
hot water, this enables us to save 
cooling water loss and recover 
energy saving fuels and eliminating 
CO2 emissions.
We have adopted an IT-based 
Energy Management System 
(EnMS) for controlling, managing 
and conserving energy. Based 
on our several energy efficiency 
initiatives, we have saved approx 
2.3 million KWH of energy in 
FY 2025-26.
AIL has started receiving 13.2 
MW of hybrid renewable energy. 
Additionally 2.75 MW of renewable 
energy is also sourced since Q3 
FY26. Further phase-2 investment 
for 25.7.MW is expected to be 
operational in FY 2026-27.
Positive

2. Does the entity have processes in place to avoid/manage conflict of interests involving members of the Board? (Yes/
No) If Yes, provide details of the same.
 The Company has a process in place which is governed by the Company’s Code of Conduct which is available on the 
website of the Company. For the purpose of this Code of Conduct, the term “Employees” includes employees, associates, 
officers, and directors of AIL and its subsidiaries. The Company’s Code of Conduct emphasises the principles of loyalty, 
integrity, and ethical business conduct. All employees are expected to act solely in the interests of the Company within 
the scope of their employment and ensure that personal, financial, or other business interests do not interfere with, or 
appear to interfere with, the interests of the Company. The Code of Conduct requires employees to avoid situations 
that may give rise to actual, potential, or perceived conflicts of interest. A conflict of interest exists when an employee’s 
actions or private interests interfere, or appear to interfere, with the interests of the Company.
 Every Director of the Company also discloses his/her concern or interest in the Company or companies or bodies 
corporate or firms or other association of individuals and any change therein, annually or upon any change, which also 
includes the shareholding. In the Meetings of the Board, the Directors abstain from participating in the matters in which 
they are concerned or interested.
 The Corporate Secretarial team also maintains a database of the Directors and the entities in which they are interested 
for identifying and tracking conflict of interests which is shared with the Finance department which flags off the parties 
in their system for monitoring and tracking transaction(s) entered by the Company with such parties.

b

 Anchored by our ‘Zero Harm’ philosophy, AIL utilises a suite of advanced diagnostic tools to proactively identify work-
related hazards and manage operational risks. Routine operations are governed by a Hazard Identification and Risk 
Assessment (HIRA) protocol, while non-routine tasks are strictly subjected to Job Safety Analysis (JSA) to enforce 
immediate mitigation controls. At the engineering level, process safety is institutionalised through comprehensive 
risk registers and barrier management systems that track the healthiness of critical safeguards against top-tier 
risks. Furthermore, our design lifecycle integrates rigorous process safety studies—spanning Thermal Safety (DSC, 
TSu, RC1e), Powder Safety, Criticality Classifications, SIL, QRA, and HAC. These internal frameworks are validated 
through independent audits led by external specialists and reported to regulatory authorities, ensuring continual 
risk reduction and reinforced safety capabilities backed by organisational tacit knowledge.

‘General Plant Condition’ module, which allows anyone on-site to log unsafe acts and conditions for prompt 
operational intervention. Parallelly, our occupational health and safety protocols ensure a strict non-retaliation 
policy regarding personal safety; workers have the right to refuse unsafe work or evacuate a high-risk area if they 
encounter an immediate hazard, ensuring that human well-being is systematically prioritised over operational

10. Briefly describe the waste management practices adopted in your establishments. Describe the strategy adopted by 
your Company to reduce usage of hazardous and toxic chemicals in your products and processes and the practices 
adopted to manage such wastes.
 We are in the process of manufacturing specialty chemicals that are hazardous in nature. By the nature of chemistry 
itself, our operations are subjected to the generation of hazardous waste. Our R&D and technology management 
teams continuously strive to reduce waste generation by improving the performance of existing technologies and 
considering the principles of sustainability in the design of new products. We have adopted standardised protocols for 
waste identification and categorisation, waste collection and segregation, labelling, storage, and responsible disposal 
of hazardous and non-hazardous waste. Our waste management policies are intended to handle hazardous and non-
hazardous waste in accordance with legal requirements and globally accepted best practices.
 Our waste management approach is systematically divided into three priorities depending upon the various operating 
conditions and type of waste generated. These are as follows:
 Measures taken to minimise primary pollution, waste prevention and our priority to reduce hazardous waste are:
 • Change industrial process to eliminate use of harmful chemicals
 • Use less of a harmful/product
 • Reduce packaging and materials in products
 • Make products last longer and are recyclable, reusable, or easy to repair
 • Change industrial processes to reduce or eliminate hazardous waste production
 Measures taken to minimise secondary pollution and waste prevention and second priority to reduce Hazardous or Non-
Hazardous waste are:
 • Reuse
 • Recovery
 • Recycle
 • Repair
 • Buy reusable and recyclable products
 Treatment and disposal of all our waste:
 • Treating waste to reduce toxicity
 • Incinerate waste
 • Waste in landfills
 • Co- processing

5. Does the entity have a business continuity and disaster management plan? Give details in 100 words/web link.
 Yes. The Company has a Business Continuity Plan and Disaster Management Plan to defend against physical and 
operational disruptions. Physical emergencies are countered via facility-specific On-Site and Off-Site Emergency 
Plans (OSEP), featuring clear escalation hierarchies, dedicated crisis infrastructure, and continuous workforce safety 
drills. Concurrently, our business continuity protocols mitigate enterprise-level risks. This comprehensive governance 
framework guarantees the safety of our workforce while ensuring operational stability and uninterrupted delivery during 
unforeseen crises.
6. Disclose any significant adverse impact to the environment, arising from the value chain of the entity. What mitigation 
or adaptation measures have been taken by the entity in this regard.
 While no significant adverse environmental impacts were recorded across our value chain during the reporting period, 
AIL remains aware of the high energy intensity of our raw material supply chain. To map climate risks and target emission 
hotspots, the Company has executed Product Carbon Footprint (PCF) studies for more than 80% of its goods by spend. 
In response to these findings, our value chain mitigation and adaptation frameworks focus on collaborative supplier 
engagement, driving logistics efficiencies, and promoting the adoption of a diverse, renewable energy mix to actively 
reduce Scope 3 emissions.

AUSE (i) OF SUBSECTION 3 OF SECTION 143 OF THE 
COMPANIES ACT, 2013 (THE “ACT”)
We have audited the internal financial controls with 
reference to standalone financial statements of Aarti 
Industries Limited (the “Company”) as of March 31, 2026 
in conjunction with our audit of the standalone financial 
statements of the Company for the year ended on that date.
OPINION
In our opinion, to the best of our information and according 
t
o the explanations given to us, the Company has, in all 
material respects, an adequate internal financial controls 
system with reference to standalone financial statements 
and such internal financial controls with reference to 
standalone financial statements were operating effectively 
as at March 31, 2026, based on the criteria for internal 
financial control over financial reporting established by the 
Company considering the essential components of internal 
control stated in the Guidance Note on Audit of Internal 
Financial Controls Over Financial Reporting issued by the 
ICAI.
MANAGEMENTS’ RESPONSIBILITY FOR INTERNAL FINANCIAL 
CONTROLS
The Company’s Management is responsible for establishing 
and maintaining internal financial controls with reference 
to standalone financial statements based on the internal 
control over financial reporting criteria established by the 
Company considering the essential components of internal 
control stated in the Guidance Note on Audit of Internal 
Financial Controls Over Financial Reporting issued by the 
Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (the “ICAI”). 
These responsibilities include the design, implementation 
and maintenance of adequate internal financial controls 
that were operating effectively for ensuring the orderly 
and efficient conduct of its business, including adherence 
to company’s policies, the safeguarding of its assets, the 
prevention and detection of frauds and errors, the accuracy 
and completeness of the accounting records, and the timely 
preparation of reliable financial information, as required 
under the Act.
AUDITORS’ RESPONSIBILITY
Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the Company’s 
internal 
financial controls with reference to standalone 
financial statements based on our audit. We conducted 
our audit in accordance with the Guidance Note on Audit 
of Internal Financial Controls Over Financial Reporting (the 
“Guidance Note”) issued by the ICAI and the Standards on 
Auditing prescribed under Section 143(10) of the Act, to the 
extent applicable to an audit of internal financial controls 
with reference to financial statements. Those Standards 
and the Guidance Note require that we comply with ethical 
requirements and plan and perform the audit to obtain 
reasonable assurance about whether adequate internal 
financial controls with reference to financial statements was 
established and maintained and if such controls operated 
effectively in all material respects. Our audit involves 
performing procedures to obtain audit evidence about the 
adequacy of the internal financial controls with reference 
to standalone financial statements and their operating 
effectiveness. Our audit of internal financial controls with 
reference to financial statements included obtaining an 
understanding of internal financial controls with reference 
to financial statements, assessing the risk that a material 
weakness exists, and testing and evaluating the design 
and operating effectiveness of internal control based on 
the assessed risk. The procedures selected depend on 
the auditor’s judgement, including the assessment of the 
risks of material misstatement of the financial statements, 
whether due to fraud or error. We believe that the audit 
evidence we have obtained, is sufficient and appropriate 
to provide a basis for our audit opinion on the Company’s 
internal financial controls with reference to standalone 
financial statements. 
MEANING OF INTERNAL FINANCIAL CONTROLS WITH 
REFERENCE T
O STANDALONE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
A company’s internal financial control over financial 
reporting is a process designed to provide reasonable 
assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting 
and the preparation of standalone financial statements for 
external purposes in accordance with generally accepted 
accounting principles. A company’s internal financial 
control over financial reporting includes those policies and 
procedures that 
• pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable 
detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and 
dispositions of the assets of the Company;
• provide reasonable assurance that transactions 
ar
e recorded as necessary to permit preparation of 
standalone Ind AS financial statements in accordance 
with generally accepted accounting principles, and

2. MATERIAL ACCOUNTING POLICIES
(A) BASIS OF PREPARATION AND PRESENTATION:
 The Standalone Financial Statements have been 
prepared in accordance with the accounting 
principles generally accepted in India including Indian 
Accounting Standards (Ind AS) prescribed under 
Section 133 of the Companies Act, 2013, read with 
rule 3 of Companies (Indian Accounting Standards) 
Rules, 2015 as amended and relevant provisions of 
the Companies Act, 2013 including presentation and 
disclosure requirements of Division II of Schedule III of 
the Act as amended from time to time.
 Accordingly, the Company has prepared 
these  Standalone Financial Statements which 
comprise the Balance Sheet as at 31st March, 2026, 
the Statement of Profit and Loss for the year ended 
31st March, 2026, the Statement of Cash Flows for 
the year ended 31st March, 2026 and the Statement 
of Changes in Equity for the year ended as on that 
date, and accounting policies and other explanatory 
information (together hereinafter referred to as ‘ 
Standalone Financial Statements’).
 These Standalone Financial Statements have been 
prepared on a going concern basis; the management 
having assessed that the Company has adequate 
resources to continue in operational existence for the 
foreseeable future.
 In addition, the Standalone financial statements 
are presented in INR which is also the Company’s 
functional currency and  all values are rounded to the 
nearest crore except when otherwise indicated.
(B) BASIS OF MEASUREMENT:
 The Standalone financial statements are prepared 
in accordance with Indian Accounting Standards 
(Ind AS), under the historical cost convention on the 
accrual basis as per the provisions of the Companies 
Act, 2013 (“the Act”), except for:
 - Financial instruments – measured at fair value;
 - Plan assets under defined benefit plans – 
measured at fair value
 - Equity-settled share-based payments - measured 
at fair value at the grant date;
 - Other long-term employee benefits - measured at 
the present value of the defined benefit obligation.
 In addition, the carrying values of recognised assets 
and liabilities, designated as hedged items in fair 
value hedges that would otherwise be carried at cost, 
are adjusted to record changes in the fair values 
attributable to the risks that are being hedged in 
effective hedge relationships.
(C) SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES, 
JUDGEMENTS AND ASSUMPTIONS:
 The preparation of the Standalone financial statements 
in conformity with Ind AS requires the management to 
make estimates, judgments and assumptions. These 
estimates, judgments and assumptions affect the 
application of accounting policies and the reported 
amounts of assets and liabilities, the disclosures of 
contingent assets and liabilities at the date of the 
financial statements and reported amounts of revenues 
and expenses during the period. Actual results could 
differ from those estimates according to the nature of 
the assumption and other circumstances. This note 
provides an overview of the areas where there is a higher 
degree of judgment or complexity. Detailed information 
about each of these estimates and judgments is 
included in relevant notes together with information 
about the basis of calculation.
 The following are areas involving critical estimates 
and judgments:
 Judgements:
 - Leases
 - Evaluation of recoverability of deferred tax 
assets, and estimation of income tax payable and 
income tax expense in relation to an uncertain tax 
position
 - Provisions and Contingencies
 - Determination of the point at which control of 
exported goods transfers to the customer, having

(D) CURRENT AND NON-CURRENT CLASSIFICATION:
 The Company presents assets and liabilities in 
the Balance Sheet based on current/non-current 
classification, An assets is treated as current when it 
is:
 i) Expected to be realised or intended to be sold or 
consumed in normal operating cycle, or
 ii) Held primarily for the purpose of trading, or
 iii) Expected to be realised within twelve months 
after the reporting period, or
 iv) Cash or cash equivalent unless restricted from 
being exchanged or used to settle a liability for at 
least twelve months after the reporting period
 A liability is treated as current when it is:
 (i) Expected to be settled in normal operating cycle, 
or
 (ii) Held primarily for the purpose of trading, or
 (iii) Due to be settled within twelve months after the 
reporting period, or
 (iv) There is no unconditional right to defer the 
settlement of the liability for at least twelve 
months after the reporting period
 All other assets and liabilities are classified as non-
current assets and liabilities. Deferred tax assets and 
liabilities are classified as non-current assets and 
liabilities.
 The operating cycle is the time between the acquisition 
of assets for processing and their realisation in cash 
and cash equivalents. The Company has identified 
twelve months as its operating cycle.
(E) PROPERTY, PLANT AND EQUIPMENT, INTANGIBLE 
ASSETS AND DEPRECIATION/AMORTIZATION:
 1. Property, Plant and Equipment (PPE)
 PPEs held for use in the production, supply or 
administr
ative purposes, are stated in the balance 
sheet at cost less applicable accumulated 
depreciation/amortisation and accumulated 
impairment losses (if any).
 The cost of PPE comprises its purchase price 
(including the costs of materials/components) 
net of any trade discounts and rebates, any 
import duties and other taxes (other than 
those subsequently recoverable from the tax 
authorities), any directly attributable expenditure 
on making the asset ready for its intended use, 
including relevant borrowing costs for qualifying 
assets including exchange differences arising 
from foreign currency borrowings to the extent 
that they are regarded as an adjustment to interest 
costs and such other incidental costs that may 
be associated with acquisition or creation of the 
asset ready for its intended use.
 An item or part of PPE is derecognised upon 
disposal or when no future economic benefits are 
expected from its use. Any gain or loss arising 
on de-recognition of the asset (calculated as the 
difference between the net disposal proceeds 
and the carrying amount of the asset) is included 
in the Statement of Profit & Loss as and when the 
asset is derecognised.
 PPE which are not ready for intended use as 
on the date of Balance Sheet are disclosed 
as “Capital work-in-progress”. Capital Work-
in-Progress represents expenditure incurred 
on capital assets that are under construction/
erection or are pending to be commercialised and 
put to use. The same is carried at cost which is 
determined in the same manner as for any PPE.
 2. Intangible Assets
 Intangible assets are recognised when it is 
pr
obable that the future economic benefits 
that are attributable to the asset will flow to 
the Company and the cost of the asset can be 
measured reliably. Intangible assets are stated 
at original cost net of tax/duty credits availed, 
if any, less accumulated amortisation and 
cumulative impairment. Administrative and other

 The Company assesses at each reporting date

(F) RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT:
 Research costs are expensed as incurred. 
Development expenditures on an individual project are 
recognised as an intangible asset when the Company

 - future economic benefits are probable; and

resources to complete development and to use or 
sell the asset.

expenditure as an asset, the asset is carried at cost 
less any accumulated amortisation and accumulated 
impairment losses. Amortisation of the asset begins 
when development is complete and the asset is 
available for use. It is amortised over the period of 
expected future benefit. Amortisation expense is 
recognised in the statement of profit and loss unless

(I) REVENUE RECOGNITION:
 Ind AS 115 applies, with limited exceptions, to all 
revenue arising from contracts with its customers Ind 
AS 115 establishes a five-step model to account for 
revenue arising from contracts with customers and 
requires that revenue be recognised at an amount that 
reflects the consideration to which an entity expects 
to be entitled in exchange for transferring goods or 
services to a customer.
 Ind AS 115 requires entities to exercise judgment, 
taking into consideration all of the relevant facts and 
circumstances when applying each step of the model 
to contracts with their customers It also specifies the 
accounting for the incremental costs of obtaining a 
contract and the costs directly related to fulfilling a 
contract.
 (i) Sale of Goods
 Revenue from sale of goods is recognised when 
contr
ol of the products being sold is transferred 
to the customer and when there are no longer 
any unfulfilled obligations. Income from services 
rendered is recognised based on agreements/
arrangements with the customers as the 
service is performed and there are no unfulfilled 
obligations.
 The Company recognises net revenue from 
goods sold and services rendered at Transaction 
Price which is the amount of consideration the 
Company expects to be entitled to in exchange 
for transferring promised goods or services to 
a customer, excluding the amounts collected 
on behalf of a third party. The Transaction price 
is net of discounts, sales incentives, rebates 
granted, returns, sales taxes, GST and duties and 
any other recoverable taxes.
 Variable consideration, including discounts, sales

 In the case of domestic sales, the performance

the performance obligation is satisfied at the

the customer under the applicable Incoterm. 
Accordingly, where goods are sold on terms such 
as FOB, CFR and CIF, revenue is recognised by

(J) FINANCIAL INSTRUMENTS:
 Recognition and initial measurement
 Financial assets and financial liabilities are recognised 
when 
an entity becomes a party to the contractual 
provisions of the instrument. Financial assets and 
financial liabilities are initially measured at fair value. 
However, Trade receivables that do not contain 
a significant financing component are measured 
at transaction price. Transaction costs directly 
attributable to the acquisition of financial assets or 
financial liabilities at fair value through profit and 
loss are recognised immediately in the Statement of 
Profit and Loss. Transaction costs that are directly 
attributable to the acquisition or issue of financial 
assets and financial liabilities (other than financial 
assets and financial liabilities at fair value through 
Statement of Profit and Loss (FVTPL)) are added 
to or deducted from the fair value of the financial 
assets or financial liabilities, as appropriate, on initial 
recognition.
 Classification and Subsequent Measurement of 
Financial Assets:
 The Company classifies financial assets, subsequently 
at 
amortised cost, Fair Value through Other 
Comprehensive Income (“FVTOCI”) or Fair Value 
through Profit or Loss (“FVTPL”) on the basis of 
following:
 - the entity’s business model for managing the 
financial assets and
 - the contractual cash flow characteristics of the 
financial asset.
 (a) Financial Assets measured at Amortised Cost:
 A Financial Asset is measured at amortised 
Cost if it is held within a business model whose 
objective is to hold the asset in order to collect 
contractual cash flows and the contractual terms 
of the Financial Asset give rise on specified dates 
to cash flows that represent solely payments of 
principal and interest on the principal amount 
outstanding.
 (b) Financial Assets measured at Fair Value Through 
Other Comprehensive Income (FVTOCI):
 A Financial Asset is measured at FVTOCI if it is 
held within a business model whose objective 
is achieved by both collecting contractual cash 
flows and selling Financial Assets and the 
contractual terms of the Financial Asset give rise 
on specified dates to cash flows that represent 
solely payments of principal and interest on the 
principal amount outstanding.
 (c) Financial Assets measured at Fair Value Through 
Profit or Loss (FVTPL):
 FVTPL is a residual category for financial assets. 
Any financial asset, which does not meet the 
criteria for categorisation as at amortised cost or 
as FVTOCI, is classified as at FVTPL.
